passage: In Kalimpong, the monsoon had closed the main road for a week, and the nursing students walked an hour down the hill to the district hospital for their practicals. Tenzin had chosen nursing after a year of working at her aunt's pharmacy and watching the night nurses. She knew what she was signing up for. Binita, walking beside her with a torn umbrella, had joined because her parents said it was a safe government job. By Thursday Binita was talking about dropping out. "Why don't you hate this?" she asked, mud to her ankles. Tenzin thought about it. "I do hate the mud. But I picked this. Every time I'm tired, I remember why." Binita was quiet for the rest of the walk.

qa.q: How long did the nursing students walk to the district hospital?
qa.a: They walked an hour down the hill for their practicals.

qa.q: Why is Tenzin able to keep going despite the mud?
qa.a: Tenzin chose nursing after a year of watching night nurses, so the goal feels like her own and gives her a reason when she's tired.

qa.q: What could Binita do with her doubts this week?
qa.a: She could take time to think about what she actually wants, maybe talking to a senior nurse or counsellor, rather than quitting or pushing on blindly.

qa.q: How might Binita feel hearing 'I picked this'?
qa.a: Binita may feel a pang, realising she never picked nursing herself, which may explain why the mud feels heavier for her.

grounding: A nursing student who chose her course after reflection copes with hardship better than a classmate pushed into it.

passage: The carpentry workshop in Gothenburg was freezing in January, and Lars had a blister on every finger from hand-planing oak. He had spent his gap year trying a warehouse job, a café, and two weeks with his uncle building a boathouse before deciding: this. His friend Daniel was in second-year law because his parents were both lawyers. They met for coffee after a long week. "I failed my contracts exam," Daniel said flatly. "I don't even know if I care." Lars showed his blistered hands. "I've redone this joint five times. I'm furious. But I'll do it a sixth time tomorrow." "How?" Daniel asked. Lars thought. "Because nobody else picked this for me."

qa.q: What did Lars try during his gap year?
qa.a: A warehouse job, a café, and two weeks with his uncle building a boathouse.

qa.q: Why can Lars say he's furious but will try a sixth time?
qa.a: Because he chose carpentry after trying other things, the frustration sits on top of a goal he owns, so it doesn't make him want to quit.

qa.q: What might Daniel try next, given how he feels?
qa.a: He could take time to ask honestly whether law is his own choice, perhaps with a study adviser, before the next exam.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel hearing 'nobody else picked this for me'?
qa.a: It may sting, since his course followed his parents' path, and it may help explain why he doesn't know if he cares.

grounding: A young man in Sweden who chose his trade after trying others keeps going through setbacks, unlike a friend pushed into law.

passage: In the architecture college hostel, the night before the studio jury, the power went out at 1 a.m. Divyansh lit a candle and kept cutting foam board for his model. He had spent a year after school working on a construction site with his uncle before choosing architecture, and he'd filled a notebook with reasons. His roommate Mohit had been sent here because his father owned a building firm. Mohit sat on his bed, scrolling in the dark. "The jury will tear us apart anyway," he said. "What's the point?" Divyansh held up a crooked wall piece. "The point is I want to design schools that don't leak. That's why I'm up." At the jury, both got harsh comments. Divyansh fixed his model that weekend. Mohit didn't open his.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do when the power went out?
qa.a: He lit a candle and kept cutting foam board for his model.

qa.q: Why did Mohit ask 'What's the point?'
qa.a: Mohit was sent into architecture because of his father's firm, so without a reason of his own the jury's likely criticism made the effort feel pointless.

qa.q: What choice could Mohit make after the jury, instead of leaving the model shut?
qa.a: He could honestly ask himself whether he wants architecture, perhaps with a counsellor, and if he stays, find a reason of his own as Divyansh did.

qa.q: How might the jury's harsh comments land differently for Divyansh and Mohit?
qa.a: For Divyansh they are hurdles on a path he chose, so he fixes the model; for Mohit they confirm a path he never picked.

grounding: In a college hostel, a student who chose architecture after reflection keeps working through setbacks while a pushed roommate stalls.

passage:
Dear Salma,
Your letter asked if I regret it. Honestly, this semester has been the hardest thing I've done. Fieldwork at six in the heat, blisters, and I failed the soil chemistry mid-term. Papa still tells relatives I'm 'doing some farming course'.
But I don't regret it. Remember my gap year, the four months at the seed bank in Wardha, when I kept a notebook of every question I had? I chose this with that notebook open. Nobody picked it for me.
So when I failed soil chemistry, I didn't think 'why am I here'. I thought 'okay, what didn't I get?' I've been going to the professor's office every Thursday since.
Some batchmates who were sent here by their families have already stopped coming to class. I understand. It's harder to push through for someone else's reasons.
Write back soon,
Kiran

qa.q: Where did Kiran spend four months during the gap year?
qa.a: At the seed bank in Wardha.

qa.q: Why didn't failing soil chemistry make Kiran ask 'why am I here'?
qa.a: Kiran feels secure in the choice, made after real reflection with the notebook of questions open, so the setback felt like something to fix rather than a reason to quit.

qa.q: Which of Kiran's choices after the failed mid-term shows an owned goal at work?
qa.a: Going to the professor's office every Thursday; Kiran treats the failure as a gap to fill, because the reason for being there is personal.

qa.q: How might the batchmates who were sent by their families experience the same hard semester?
qa.a: Without a reason of their own to hold on to, the heat, blisters and failures may feel pointless, which is why some have stopped coming.

grounding: A young adult who chose agriculture after real reflection keeps going through hardship, unlike batchmates pushed into it.

passage:
You want to know the difference, Keerthana? First time round, B.Com, my uncle chose it. 'Safe, Ayesha. Safe.' I stopped going by October. Every small thing felt like a wall; one bad test and I'd skip a week.
Then I took a year off, worked at a print shop, and started drawing again at night. I made a list of what I actually liked doing, and animation was on it three times. I went to two open days. I talked to a second-year student for an hour. Then I applied.
Now? My laptop died in March. I did my storyboards by hand for six weeks in a borrowed corner of the library. I failed my first rigging assignment. I stayed up and redid it.
Same me. Same 'lazy' me, my uncle would say. The difference is that this time, it's my own decision on the line.

qa.q: How long did Ayesha do storyboards by hand after the laptop died?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: Why does Ayesha keep going this time despite the setbacks?
qa.a: Ayesha feels determined this time, having chosen animation after a year of reflection, a list and real conversations, so each setback seems worth pushing through.

qa.q: Which steps before applying made the second choice Ayesha's own, and why did they matter?
qa.a: Drawing at night, listing what Ayesha liked, visiting open days and talking to a second-year student; testing the choice first gave it roots that held through hard times.

qa.q: How might the uncle see the change between the B.Com and animation years?
qa.a: The uncle may still see the same 'lazy' person, without noticing that the effort changed once the choice became Ayesha's own.

grounding: A young adult contrasts quitting a course an uncle picked with pushing through setbacks in a course chosen after reflection.

passage: In their shared room in Melbourne, Bao and Alejandro both had brutal weeks. Bao was in second-year nursing, which she had chosen after a year of volunteering at an aged-care home and months of weighing it against teaching. Alejandro was in law because his father had been a lawyer, and his grandfather too. On Thursday night both of them had failed a practice exam. Bao sat with her notes and a cup of noodles, grumbling but rewriting the whole chart from memory. 'I picked this,' she said to no one in particular. 'So I'm fixing it.' Alejandro lay on his bed staring at the ceiling. 'Why do I even bother?' he said. 'This was never my idea.' At midnight Bao was still at her desk. Alejandro had fallen asleep with his textbook closed on his chest.

qa.q: What had Bao done before choosing nursing?
qa.a: She had volunteered for a year at an aged-care home.

qa.q: Why does Bao keep working after the failed practice exam?
qa.a: Bao feels frustrated but determined, because she chose nursing herself after real reflection, so the setback feels like hers to fix.

qa.q: What might help Alejandro find more energy?

qa.q: How does Alejandro experience the same bad night?

passage: At the agricultural college in Dharwad, the second-year field trial had gone badly: Saurabh's plot of millet had been flattened by a hailstorm, and Madhav's plot beside it had rotted after a pipe burst. Both had to start again with three weeks less. Saurabh had chosen agriculture after a year working on his uncle's farm, after long talks and a notebook full of pros and cons. Madhav was there because his father had filled in the form. In the college greenhouse on Monday, Saurabh was already resowing, sleeves rolled up, muttering about seed spacing. 'I chose this,' he told the lab assistant. 'A hailstorm doesn't change that.' Madhav turned up late, signed the register, and left after twenty minutes. 'What's the point,' he said at the door. 'It's not like I wanted this in the first place.'

qa.q: What flattened Saurabh's plot?
qa.a: A hailstorm flattened it.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh already resowing on Monday?
qa.a: He felt frustrated but steady, because he had chosen agriculture after real reflection, so the setback didn't shake his commitment.

qa.q: What could help Madhav through the same setback?

passage:
Dear Alka Di,
You asked how second year is going. Honestly, it's been the hardest month of my life. The jury tore apart my housing design on Friday: three professors, forty minutes, a lot of red ink. I cried in the washroom, not going to lie.
But here's the strange part. I was back at my desk by Sunday, redrawing the plan. I think it's because I remember choosing this. That gap year, the site visits with your firm, the long nights we talked about whether I really wanted architecture or just liked drawing. I chose it with open eyes. So when it hurts, it hurts like my own thing, not like something done to me.
A classmate who came here because her parents insisted is talking about dropping out. I understand her. I just feel lucky I get to fight for something I picked.
Zeenat

qa.a: The jury tore it apart on Friday.

qa.q: Why was Zeenat back at the desk by Sunday despite crying?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt but also determined, because having chosen architecture after real reflection, the setback felt like part of Zeenat's own path, not something imposed.

passage:
You asked how I kept going in nursing when half my batch dropped out, Zainab. Let me tell you.
I'm Gurleen. In Class 12 everyone expected me to do engineering. I spent that whole summer volunteering at the Civil Hospital in Ludhiana, just to see. I sat with old patients, held hands during dressings, watched the nurses work double shifts.
Then I chose nursing. Not because I was told to. Because I'd seen it, the hard parts too.
Second year was brutal. Night duties, a patient I'd grown fond of died, and I failed pharmacology the first time.
My friend Tanu, who was pushed into it by her parents, quit that year. I understood why.
But every time I wanted to stop, I'd remember that summer. I chose this with my eyes open. That kept me standing. I passed pharmacology on the second go.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen volunteer the summer after Class 12?
qa.a: Gurleen volunteered at the Civil Hospital in Ludhiana.

qa.q: What kept Gurleen going when Gurleen felt like stopping?
qa.a: Gurleen felt steadier remembering that the choice was made with open eyes after seeing the hard parts, so the goal felt truly owned.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's story suggest about choosing a course?
qa.a: Taking time to see the real work before choosing, as Gurleen did, can build a commitment that holds through setbacks.

qa.q: How might Tanu have felt in the same brutal second year?
qa.a: Tanu, pushed into it by her parents, probably felt trapped and exhausted, with no reason of her own to keep going.

grounding: The spoken account shows a young adult who chose nursing after real reflection sustaining effort through hardship better than a friend pushed into it.

passage:
June: Manoj picked agricultural science after a summer on his uncle's farm, testing soil and talking to farmers. His roommate Kashish was there because his father owned a fertiliser shop and had filled in the form for him.
October: Their first field trial failed. Heavy rain rotted half the seedlings. Kashish threw his notebook on the bed. “Why am I even doing this?” Manoj was upset too, but he went back to the field at dawn and started recording what went wrong.
February: Kashish had missed most of the practicals and was talking about switching. Manoj had redone the trial with raised beds. It worked better. When his professor asked why he kept going after the rain, Manoj shrugged. “I wanted this before I got here. The rain didn't change that.”

qa.q: What happened to the first field trial in October?
qa.a: Heavy rain rotted half the seedlings.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after the failed trial, and why did he return at dawn?
qa.a: He felt upset, but because he had chosen the course himself after real reflection, he was determined to find out what went wrong.

qa.q: What could help Kashish now?
qa.a: Kashish could talk honestly with a counsellor and his father about what he actually wants, so any path he takes is one he owns.

qa.q: How does Kashish experience the same setback differently?

passage:
Bidisha, you're asking whether to take the architecture seat your parents want, or teaching, which you keep talking about. Let me, your Madhav Mama, tell you about two boys in 1996.
One was me. I was twenty and spent six months tutoring slum children in Howrah before deciding. I wanted to teach. My father sulked for a year.
The other was my friend Partha, who did chartered accountancy because his father said so.
In my third year the college almost shut down, we got no salary for four months during my internship, and I cried on the ferry more than once. But I'd seen those children's faces. I'd chosen it. I stayed.
Partha was brilliant, but when he failed a paper, he gave up. He said, “It was never mine anyway.”
I'm not telling you what to choose. I'm telling you: choose it yourself.

qa.q: How long did young Madhav tutor children before deciding?
qa.a: He tutored slum children in Howrah for six months before deciding.

qa.q: Why did young Madhav stay during the four months without salary?
qa.a: He felt deeply committed because he had seen the children's faces and chosen teaching himself, so the hardship didn't break his resolve.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Partha's path turn, and what might have helped him?
qa.a: When he failed a paper and gave up; time to reflect and choose his own path earlier might have helped him hold on.

qa.q: How might Partha have felt when he said “It was never mine anyway”?
qa.a: Partha probably felt defeated and resigned, with no personal reason to keep going.

passage: The floodwater was knee-deep outside the district hospital, the power kept failing, and Payal and Hrithik were on their first night shift as nursing students. Payal had chosen nursing after a year of volunteering at a clinic, thinking hard about whether she could handle blood, nights, sadness. Hrithik's parents had chosen it for him because a cousin got a job abroad. By 3 am, both were soaked and exhausted. A generator failed and they held torches for the doctor. Hrithik kept checking his phone. "I didn't sign up for this." Payal was tired too; her feet ached and her uniform was muddy. But when an old woman squeezed her hand, she thought, This is what I chose. I knew it would be hard. At dawn, Hrithik said, "I'm thinking of quitting." Payal, rubbing her eyes, said, "I'm thinking of breakfast. And coming back tomorrow."

qa.q: How deep was the floodwater outside the hospital?
qa.a: It was knee-deep.

qa.q: How did Payal feel through the hard night, and what kept her going?
qa.a: Payal was exhausted and aching but steady, because she had chosen nursing after real reflection and knew it would be hard.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do to find his own reasons for staying or leaving?
qa.a: He could take time to reflect on what he wants, perhaps by talking to a mentor, rather than staying only because his parents chose it.

qa.q: How might the old woman who squeezed Payal's hand have felt?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and grateful for Payal's care during the frightening flood night.

passage: Saurabh had spent a year after school working on his uncle's farm near Nagpur before choosing agricultural science. He'd asked farmers what they needed, read about soil, and decided. His friend Chandrika had gone into chartered accountancy because her parents insisted. Now, in their third year, both hit a wall. Saurabh failed his soil chemistry practical. Chandrika failed her intermediate exam. They met at a tea stall near the university. Chandrika was in tears. "I don't even know why I'm doing this. It's their dream." Saurabh was upset too; he'd studied hard for that practical. But he said, "I know why I'm doing mine. Uncle's cotton crop failed because the soil was wrong. I want to fix that." He paid for the tea and went straight back to the lab to ask what he'd done wrong. Chandrika watched him go, and stared at her cup for a long time.

qa.q: What did Saurabh fail in the third year?
qa.a: He failed his soil chemistry practical.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel after failing, and what kept him going?
qa.a: Saurabh was upset because he'd studied hard, but his own reason, fixing soil for farmers like his uncle, gave him the will to go straight back to the lab.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do to find her footing after this setback?
qa.a: She could reflect honestly on whether she wants CA for her own reasons, and talk openly with her parents about what she wants.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel watching Saurabh go back to the lab?
qa.a: Chandrika probably felt lost and a little envious, lacking a reason of her own to carry her through.

passage:
"Kamal, you failed the jury. Aren't you going to quit?"
"No, Manoj. I'm redoing the sculpture."
"But it's so much work. And your parents wanted you to do commerce."
"I know. I spent a whole year thinking about it before I chose fine arts. I visited three art colleges, I worked at a potter's shop. I knew it would be hard."
"And it's hard."
"Really hard. I cried after the jury."
"So?"
"So I chose this. It's mine. When it's hard, I remember why."
"I'm in engineering because Papa said so. Every time something goes wrong, I just want to leave."
"Maybe that's the difference."
"What?"
"You didn't choose it. It's hard to hold on to something that isn't yours."
Manoj was quiet. Then: "Show me the sculpture."
"It's only half-done."
"Show me anyway."

qa.a: He visited three art colleges and worked at a potter's shop.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel after failing the jury, and why isn't he quitting?
qa.a: Kamal was hurt and even cried, but he chose the path after a year of reflection, so remembering why keeps him going.

qa.q: What does the talk suggest Manoj could think about?
qa.a: Whether engineering is truly his choice, since goals pushed on him are harder to hold through setbacks.

qa.a: Manoj seemed thoughtful and a little envious, realising he never really chose his own course.

passage:
I'm Divyansh, and I spent most of a year before college deciding. I worked on my uncle's farm, visited two colleges, asked the lecturers awkward questions, and wrote down why I wanted agriculture and not the engineering everyone expected.
Then first year happened. The monsoon flooded our trial plots twice. We were up at five for field readings, mud to the knees, and my okra died anyway. Some nights I sat on the hostel steps, soaked, thinking, what have I done?
But every time, I opened that old notebook. My own handwriting: I want to know why Nanaji's soil stopped giving. And I got up the next morning.
Rekha, who joined because her father picked the college, sat on those same steps with me in August. By Diwali she had gone home. I don't think she was weaker than me. I think she was carrying someone else's reason.

qa.q: What was written in Divyansh's old notebook?
qa.a: "I want to know why Nanaji's soil stopped giving."

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel on the hostel steps, and what kept Divyansh going?
qa.a: Divyansh felt soaked, discouraged and full of doubt, but rereading a reason written in Divyansh's own hand was steadying enough to get up the next morning.

qa.q: What does Divyansh's year of deciding suggest for someone choosing a course?
qa.a: Trying the work, asking real questions and writing down one's own reasons builds a goal that can survive floods and dead crops.

qa.q: How might Rekha have experienced the same first year?
qa.a: Rekha faced the same mud and floods without a reason of her own, so each setback probably felt heavier, and she went home by Diwali.

grounding: A young adult who chose a course after real reflection keeps going through hardship, while a batchmate pushed into it leaves.
